name: Tech help at home
what_example: phone and computer help for older adults

not_yet: Don't offer remote help with screen sharing apps. Help in person.
Don't take on office networks or business IT before your tenth home client.
Don't keep, write down or store anyone's passwords, even when they ask you to.
crowd.note: Trust comes first: the client types every password, family is welcome at every visit, and every visit ends with a written note.
crowd.basis: Scores, buyer, first $1 and not-yet lines: research/niches/techhelp.json crowd_scores (our judgment, with Pew, Census and FBI IC3 sources). Best months: all year, a judgment call.

safety: Never ask for, see, write down or keep a client's passwords. They type them while you look away.
Help in person only, with no remote access apps: the FTC and Microsoft say tech support scammers ask for remote access.
Never handle their money: no gift cards, no transfers, no payments for them. You're paid by a written invoice. The FTC says no real business asks to be paid with a gift card.
No rush and no pressure: the price is in writing before the visit. The FTC says honest businesses give you time to decide.
A family member or trusted friend is always welcome, and gets the visit note with the client's okay.
Every visit ends with a written note, and the note never has a password in it.

extra.title: Phone call script (15 minutes, free)
lines: 1. Thanks for making time. Which devices do you have, and what's giving you the most trouble?
2. Does anyone in the family help now? They're welcome at the visit.
3. Here's how I work: you type your own passwords, I never use remote access, and I never ask you to buy anything or move money.
4. A visit is up to 90 minutes at your home. We start with what matters most to you, and you get a written note after the visit.
5. You pay by invoice after the visit. My founding price is {founding}.
6. Would you like to pick a day? There's no rush: take time to think it over or talk to family first.

offer.range_text: $45 to $90 an hour for computer and tech help
offer.basis: From research/niches/techhelp.json (HomeAdvisor and Thumbtack, checked 2026-10-19): about $60 an hour on average. Geek Squad lists in-home printer setup at $124.99 and home Wi-Fi setup at $174.99 per job. The 90-minute visit is our judgment.
includes: A visit plan built from your devices and what's not working
Patient help on your own devices, at your pace
A printed scam warning card from the FTC's advice
A written note after every visit: what we did, what to practice, what's next
steps: A free 15-minute phone call: which devices you have and what's giving you trouble.

You get a written note the same day, and a copy for family if you'd like.
offer.promise: If I'm late or miss a visit, the next one is free. If you're not happy with the first visit, I refund it.
offer.promise_note: I don't promise that a device will never break or that scams will stop. I promise the work: on time, at your pace, and a written note after every visit.
sheet_notes: I never ask for your passwords. You type them yourself, and I look away.
I don't use remote access apps, and I'll never call you out of the blue about a problem with your computer.

objections.label: A scam may have happened
objections.match: \b(i think i (was|got|'ve been) scammed|got scammed|was scammed|been scammed|pop-?up (said|told|on my)|called the number|let (him|her|them|someone) (in|into|on)|gave (him|her|them|someone) (access|my)|bought (the )?gift cards?|paid (with|in) gift cards?|was hacked|got hacked|been hacked)
objections.means: Something may already have happened: they paid, shared a password or let someone in.
objections.answer: I'm sorry that happened, and you're not alone. Here are the FTC's steps. If you paid by card, call your bank or card company using the number on the back of the card and ask for a refund. If you paid with a gift card, call the gift card company using the number on the back of the card. If someone got into your computer, update your security software, run a scan and change your passwords. Then report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. If you'd like a hand with any of it, just say so.
objections.next: Help with the FTC steps first. Don't quote a price in this reply.

sources.says: Card: report it using the number on the back of the card and ask for a refund. Gift card: contact the issuer using the number on the back of the card. Remote access: update security software, run a scan, change passwords.
If a tech support scammer contacts you, tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

objections.label: How do they know you're safe?
objections.match: \b(how do i know|can i trust|are you (legit|real)|is this (legit|real|a scam)|sounds like a scam|scammers?)\b
objections.means: They want to know you're not a scammer, which is the right question.
objections.answer: Good question, and the right one to ask. Here's how I work: I never ask for your passwords, you type them yourself. I never ask for remote access to your computer, and I never ask you to pay with gift cards or move money. You pay by invoice after the visit, and a family member is welcome to be there. The FTC says to get tech help from someone you know and trust, so ask around about me first if you like.
objections.next: Answer it fully, then let them take their time.

sources.says: If you need tech help, go to someone you know and trust.
No real business or government agency will ever tell you to buy a gift card to pay them.

objections.label: Can you help remotely?
objections.match: \b(remote(ly)?|over the phone|log in from|teamviewer|anydesk|screen ?shar\w*|connect to my (computer|laptop|pc))\b
objections.means: They'd like help without a visit.
objections.answer: I only help in person, at your home. I don't use remote access apps, because scammers ask people for remote access, and a stranger asking for it is a warning sign. This way you see everything I do, on your own screen.
objections.next: Offer the visit, never a remote session.

sources.says: In tech support scams, the scammers ask for remote access to your computer.
Scammers will probably ask you to install applications that give them remote access to your device.

objections.label: Do you need my passwords?
objections.means: They're asking about passwords, and the answer is no.
objections.answer: No, you keep your passwords, always. When one is needed, you type it yourself while I look away, and I never write one down or keep one. If you'd like, I can show you the password manager that's already built into your phone, so it remembers them for you.
objections.next: Say it plainly, then offer the free phone call.

sources.says: A password manager stores and fills in your passwords, so you only need to remember one strong password.
The Passwords app comes with iPhone and iPad on iOS 18 or later.
Google Password Manager saves and fills in passwords on Android and in Chrome.

objections.label: A repair, not tech help
objections.answer: That sounds like a repair, and I don't do repairs myself. A phone repair shop or the maker's own support is the right place for it. Once it's fixed, I'm glad to help move your photos and contacts, or set things up the way you like.
objections.next: Point them to a repair shop or the maker. Offer setup after.

objections.label: More than they expected
objections.means: The price feels high to them.
objections.answer: That's fair to ask. Computer and tech help runs about $45 to $90 an hour, and one in-home setup job at Geek Squad is $124.99 to $174.99. For {rate} you get up to {length} at your pace, a printed scam card and a written note after the visit. A short 45-minute visit costs less, if that suits you better.
objections.next: Hold your price. Offer the short visit.

sources.says: Computer repair technicians charge between $45 and $90 per hour.
In-home Printer Setup $124.99; Home Wi-Fi Setup $174.99.

objections.label: Family usually helps
objections.means: Someone in the family helps now.
objections.answer: That's wonderful, family help is the best kind. If they're busy or far away, I'm glad to fill in, and I'm happy to work alongside them or send them the note after each visit, with your okay.
objections.next: Offer to work with the family, then leave it there.

objections.label: Can family be there?
objections.match: \b(be there|sit in|join us|come too|be present|be with me)\b
objections.means: They'd like someone with them at the visit.
objections.answer: Of course, and I'd encourage it. Anyone you'd like is welcome at every visit, and with your okay I can send them the same note I send you.
objections.next: Say yes, and add them to the visit plan.

objections.label: Can't I get free help?
objections.means: They wonder why they'd pay when free help exists.
objections.answer: If your library or senior center has a free tech help hour, use it! I'm glad to help you find one. What I add is time at your own home, on your own devices, at your pace, with a written note after the visit.
objections.next: Agree, then offer the free phone call.

objections.label: Can you promise it's safe?
objections.match: \b(promise|guarant\w*|never get (a virus|hacked|scammed)|100 ?%|totally safe|completely safe|safe from|make sure (i|we) (never|don't|won't))\b
objections.means: They want safety or a result promised.
objections.answer: I can't promise that, and I'd be careful with anyone who does. What I can promise is the work: I show up on time, go at your pace, never ask for your passwords, and leave a written note after every visit. The scam card helps you spot the common tricks.
objections.next: Never promise safety or a fix. Offer the visit plan instead.

objections.label: References or a background check?
objections.means: They want to know who's coming into their home.
objections.answer: Good question, and the right one to ask anyone who comes to your home. Here's how I work: you type your own passwords, I never ask for remote access or money, and a family member is welcome at every visit. I'm glad to share references from people I've helped.
objections.next: Send this once you have references to share.
objections.check: Have references ready to share before you send this, and only mention a background check or insurance you really have.

win.title: Log the new client
win.description: A client said yes: logs the win in your Pipeline, writes the booking message, the prep message and the day-before reminder, and a printable first visit checklist with the visit rules.
where: At the library or senior center
win.booking: Hi {greet}, you're all set! Your first visit is {when}{where}. It's {deal}. Please have your devices and chargers out, and anyone you'd like is welcome to be there.
win.prep: Before the visit, could you jot down which devices you'd like help with and what's not working? Please don't write down any passwords: you'll type them yourself when we need them.
win.reminder: Hi {greet}, see you {when}. I'll text when I'm on my way. If anything changes, just reply here, and we'll find another day.
win.founding: Founding client: after the first visit, ask {greet} for honest feedback you may quote as a founding client. Never ask for a review in exchange.

Before: Confirm the day, time and place with the client in writing.
Agree the price, what it covers and the cancellation rule in writing, before the visit.
Ask which devices and problems to look at, then run Visit plan and scam card.
Print the scam card to leave with them.
At the visit: Meet anyone they asked to be there. Ask before you open email, photos, messages or money apps.
The client types every password while you look away. Never write one down, photograph it or save it.
No remote access apps, no gift cards, no money moves and no sign-ups on their behalf.
Start with what matters most to them, then let them practice it on their own device.
Go over the scam card together and put it by the phone.
After: Send the visit note the same day: what you did, what to practice and what's next.
Send a copy to family only with the client's okay.
Book the next visit only if they want one. No pressure.

sources.says: Tech support scammers ask for remote access and insist on gift cards, wire transfers or payment apps.
Honest businesses will give you time to make a decision.
Rather than write passwords down, use a password manager (archived page).
